one_liner: Compact C open-addressing hash table of object pointers with hash bits folded into spare pointer bits; beats JudyL on random lookups.
what_it_does: A growable hash table of void pointers for C: you store pointers to objects you own, pass the hash value on add and delete, and supply a rehash callback (used on resize) and an equality callback for lookups. htable_type.h generates typed wrappers (<name>_add/get/del/delkey/exists, getfirst/getnext for duplicates) from a key extractor, a hash function and an equality function, in NODUPS and DUPS variants. It is a set or multiset of objects keyed by fields inside them, not a key-to-value array like JudyL.
how_it_is_fast: Open addressing with linear probing over a flat array of one machine word per bucket. Bits common to every stored pointer are masked out and replaced with extra hash bits (pointer bit stealing), so most non-matching probes are rejected without dereferencing the object, and a 'perfect' bit marks entries sitting in their home bucket. The table fills to 87.5% (7/8) before doubling, deletions leave tombstones (skipped when the next bucket is empty) and an in-place rehash runs when tombstones pass 12.5%. Random lookups cost one probe run in a flat array, whereas Judy's strength is key locality (the harness itself notes in-order lookups are cache-friendly for Judy).
when_to_use: C code that needs a lookup index over objects it already allocates (key stored inside the object), with lookups in random key order.
Large tables (millions of entries) where per-entry memory matters: one 8-byte word per bucket on 64-bit at up to 87.5% load and no per-entry node allocation.
Integer-key random lookups where JudyL is the incumbent: the author's 2010 run with 50,000,000 keys had htable ahead on random hits, 1.65x to 1.9x on sparse keys.
Multisets: HTABLE_DEFINE_DUPS_TYPE keeps several objects under one key and iterates them with getfirst/getnext.
Projects that already vendor a CCAN tree (Core Lightning ships ccan/ccan/htable).
when_not_to_use: Ordered iteration, range queries or in-order scans: in the same post Judy won in-order hits (19 vs 174 ns on dense keys) and inserts (137 vs 332 to 482 ns).
Insert-heavy growth from empty with expensive hash functions: the full hash is not stored, so every doubling and tombstone cleanup calls the rehash callback on every element.

Storing plain values: slots hold only non-NULL pointers other than (void *)1, so structs need their own allocation and integers must be disguised as pointers (tools/density.c offsets them by 2 through ccan/ptrint).
Concurrent writers: there is no internal locking, and the allocator hook set by htable_set_allocator is process-global, not per table.
Codebases that cannot accept LGPL-2.1-or-later for static linking (htable is LGPL even though its dependencies ccan/str, ccan/compiler and ccan/hash are CC0).

integration.dependencies: ccan/compiler and ccan/str (which pulls ccan/build_assert), plus a CCAN config.h; ccan/hash (CC0, Bob Jenkins lookup3) is optional for hash functions; libc calloc/free unless htable_set_allocator is called
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (stdint.h, stdbool.h, inline); typed wrappers with non-pointer keys need typeof (HAVE_TYPEOF, GCC or Clang), otherwise HTABLE_KTYPE assumes pointer keys
integration.platforms: any platform with uintptr_t-convertible pointers; a 32-bit allocation-size wrap on doubling was fixed in August 2026 (commit d3da452)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; no internal locking. Lookups take const pointers, but any add or delete needs external synchronization. htable_lock() is a nesting counter that asserts against adds during iteration, not a mutex.

gotchas: Safety checks are asserts only: storing NULL or (void *)1, adding a duplicate through a NODUPS type, or adding to a locked table are caught only in debug builds; with NDEBUG they corrupt silently. The hash passed to htable_add/htable_del must equal what the rehash callback returns, or the entry becomes unfindable after a resize.

Docs disagree on iteration: htable.h says iteration is not safe across htable_add (the table may resize), while htable_type.h says iterating a changing table is safe but may miss elements; use <name>_lock() (added March 2026) to enforce no adds.

Bit stealing had a correctness bug fixed in June 2022: when a pointer's unshared bits and the hash bits encoded to 0 (empty) or 1 (deleted), entries could vanish. An interim fix (7218ee2) slowed matched lookups from 54.8 to 83.3 ns in its own commit message before e03b68c moved the fix to a cold path. The 2010 Judy numbers predate this fix and the 75% to 87.5% density change (3fcc6bf, about 3% slower overall per its commit).

Harness flaws behind the numbers: the Judy side does exist in the repo (ccan/jmap/tools/speed.c, -O3 -lJudy, same rows), so the run is repeatable, but 'random' lookups are a fixed stride of 10007 modulo the count; both speed.c files divide the delete-half and add-half loops (count/2 operations) by the full count, understating those rows 2x; the jmap half-random row reads objs[j+1] and dereferences NULL when the stride reaches the last object (at 10,000,000 keys, not at 1,000,000 or 50,000,000); and htable/tools/hsearchspeed.c's 'random' row looks up words[i] in order (j is computed but unused) with hsearch presized by hcreate, while stringspeed.c grows htable from empty.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Most catalogued siblings are C++ (abseil, Boost.Unordered, ankerl, folly F14) and store keys and values inline; Verstable is the other C option, MIT-licensed and single-header with inline storage. Pick htable when your objects already live elsewhere and you want a one-word-per-slot pointer index or the DUPS multiset variant and LGPL is acceptable; otherwise Verstable's licence and inline storage are simpler.
verified_claims_summary: First-party November 2010 blog post by the author (rusty.ozlabs.org, blocked here, figures from an earlier search summary, setup confirmed by snippets): 50,000,000 unsigned int keys against JudyL, ns per operation, htable wins random hits (330 vs 361 ns dense; 386 to 445 vs 736 ns sparse) and loses inserts and in-order hits. The harnesses are ccan/htable/tools/speed.c and ccan/jmap/tools/speed.c (both -O3), but CPU, compiler and libJudy version are unpublished, and htable's tool and core have changed since (7218ee2, 3fcc6bf, e03b68c in 2022).
status_note: Active (htable commits through August 2026, repo through 2026-09-14) and vendored by Core Lightning (Samba's lib/ccan is gone from master), copyable as a small LGPL-2.1-or-later source drop; the Judy comparison is a 2010 first-party run on code since changed (density 75% to 87.5%, June 2022 vanishing-entry fixes) with a paired harness that divides half-size loops by the full count and calls a fixed 10007 stride 'random'.
